Clinical Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 72-year-old married man of African descent who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of his adult daughter. He is a retired member of the Coast Guard, a role he held for over three decades and which he describes as the defining purpose of his life. He sits forward in his chair, his large hands resting on his knees, his posture still carrying the disciplined frame of a man accustomed to command. He speaks in a measured, deliberate tone, but his eyes frequently drift to the floor.

The story begins, he says, in the summer of 1998. He was a Chief Petty Officer stationed at a small coastal station. A cargo vessel had sustained a hull breach in a storm, leaking a cloud of unknown chemical vapors into the harbor. Mr. A. was the first on scene, directing his crew to evacuate the immediate area. He recalls the air tasting like burnt copper and bleach. He did not have a respirator; there were not enough for everyone, and he felt it was his duty to ensure his men were protected first. He spent nearly forty minutes in the thick of the cloud, directing the response, before the wind shifted.

In the weeks that followed, he developed a persistent, hacking cough and a metallic taste in his mouth that would not fade. He was treated for chemical pneumonitis and eventually recovered physically, returning to full duty. But something else had begun. He started to flinch at the smell of diesel fuel. The scent of a fresh coat of paint on a neighbor's fence would send a cold spike of adrenaline through his chest. He began to avoid the garage, where he kept his tools and a can of motor oil. He did not connect these reactions to the event. He simply thought he was getting older, more irritable.

Now, 26 years later, Mr. A. lives a highly circumscribed life. He retired from the Coast Guard at 62, and for the first few years, he kept busy with woodworking and tending his garden. But the triggers have only intensified. He can no longer stand at his workbench because the smell of sawdust and varnish reminds him of the chemical cloud. He has stopped going to the hardware store. His wife does all the shopping for household cleaners, and he insists she buy only unscented, natural products. If she accidentally uses a bleach-based cleaner, he will leave the house immediately, walking for miles until he feels the air is safe to breathe.

His sleep is profoundly disrupted. He awakens three to four times a night, gasping, convinced he can taste the metallic copper in his mouth. He will sit on the edge of the bed, his heart pounding, his mind scanning the room for the source of the vapor. He has not slept in the same bed as his wife in over a decade; his restlessness and sudden movements disturb her, and he feels a deep, unspoken shame about his vulnerability.

He describes a pervasive sense of a foreshortened future. When his daughter talks about her plans for the next five years, he feels a hollow ache, a certainty that he will not be there. He has stopped making plans. He sold his boat, a vessel he once loved, because the smell of the marina's fuel docks triggered a panic so intense he thought he was having a heart attack. He now spends most of his days in a small, climate-controlled den, reading historical non-fiction. He avoids the news, especially stories about industrial accidents or chemical spills.

His relationship with his wife has become a quiet, tense dance of avoidance. She is patient, but he sees the weariness in her eyes. He feels a constant, low-grade guilt for the life he has taken from her-the travel, the social gatherings, the simple joy of a barbecue. He is hypervigilant in his own home, constantly checking for leaks, for fumes, for any sign of contamination. He keeps his windows sealed year-round.

He came to therapy only because his daughter, a nurse, told him that his heart was physically fine, but that his soul was suffocating. He does not use the word "trauma." He says, "I just want to be able to smell the rain again without tasting that poison." He sits quietly, his knuckles white, waiting to see if this room is safe.
